story.title: The Interview with Pash
story.goalShort: I want to point Army security at Eltenton without naming friends I know are innocent.
story.goalFull: I want to point Army security at Eltenton and at the Soviet back door. I will not hand them the names of friends I know are innocent.

facts: I walked into Johnson's office and was introduced to Pash, a stranger whose reputation had reached me first. It was clear he would run the interview.

He opened with compliments: General Groves had placed a responsibility in him, and it was like having a child you can't see, by remote control. I told him whatever time he chose was perfectly all right.
When he asked about my talk with Johnson, I went to Lomanitz instead: I didn't know whether I should talk to Rossi, but I wanted to tell him he had been indiscreet.
Pash cut me off. He had more serious concerns: were there other groups interested in the Rad Lab?

I told Pash I thought it was true that other groups were interested, though I had no firsthand knowledge, and described a man attached to the Soviet consul offering to transmit information without danger of leak or scandal.

I said frankly I would feel friendly to the Commander in Chief informing the Russians we were working on this problem, but not to having it moved out the back door, and it might not hurt to be on the lookout.
Pash asked evenly for more specific information. I said the approaches were always to other people, who were troubled by them and sometimes came to discuss them with me.

I told him Eltenton of Shell Development should be watched: he has probably been asked to do what he can to provide information. I said that since it is not a communication which ought to be taking place, it is treasonable.

When Pash pressed me to name who had been approached, I politely refused: the individuals were entirely innocent. I told him I knew of two or three cases, two of them men very closely associated with me at Los Alamos, and a third headed for Site X.

I would not name the third party, only that he was on the Berkeley faculty. I said it would be a mistake, that I'd told him where the initiative came from, and that the intermediary thought it was the wrong idea. I said, I don't think he supported it. In fact, I know it.

Pash said he might have to come back and press me again for more names. I told him I was only trying to act reasonably and draw the line between Eltenton, who took the initiative, and those who reacted against it.
He tried a little irony: I am not persistent, ha ha. I told him, You are persistent, and it is your duty.
I told Pash that association with the Communist movement is not compatible with the job on a secret war project; the two loyalties cannot go together.

I said a lot of brilliant and thoughtful people have seen something in the Communist movement, that maybe they belong there, maybe it is a good thing for the country, and I hope it doesn't belong on the war project.

I cited Lomanitz, for whom I still feel a sense of responsibility, and argued that everyone involved except the Russian was making up for a couple of men in the State Department who might block communication. With the Nazis, I said, it would have a somewhat different color.
Pash listened patiently, then brought the conversation back to Eltenton and the unnamed intermediary.
I came back to FAECT and told Pash there were some things there that would bear watching, and that it wouldn't hurt to have a man in the local to see what he could pick up.
He asked at once whether I knew anyone in the union who might serve as an informant. I said no; I'd only heard that a boy called Fox was president.
I told him everything at Los Alamos was 100 percent in order, that I thought that was the truth, and that I would be perfectly willing to be shot if I had done anything wrong.
When he said he might visit Los Alamos, I told him my motto was God bless you. As I rose to leave, he said the best of luck, and I said, Thank you very much.
